beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Intro to GPUs on Explorer. What a GPU is for, which ones Explorer has, and how to ask for one in a job, so the right work lands on the right hardware.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Ciao. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. A GPU is not a faster CPU. It's thousands of small, simple cores working at once, which is why it wins at some jobs and loses at others. This lecture is the beginner's introduction to the GPUs on Northeastern's Explorer cluster: which partitions and card types there are, what a GPU is, the three ways to get one, how to watch it work, and the two code habits that keep it busy.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A core: one processing unit that runs instructions on its own. A GPU: a chip with thousands of small cores for parallel work. A partition: a named group of cluster nodes with its own limits. GRES: generic resources, Slurm's name for the GPUs you ask for. s run: the command that gives you a live session on a node. And s batch: the command that submits a script to run without you.

beats.narration_text: Start with where the GPUs are. Explorer groups its GPU nodes into partitions, and six are the ones you'll meet. gpu, the general one, up to eight hours. gpu-interactive, for Open OnDemand sessions, two hours. gpu-short, two hours too, but prioritised, so quick tests schedule fast. multigpu, for jobs that need several cards, twenty-four hours. courses-gpu, for classes, twenty-four hours. And sharing: GPUs that Northeastern PIs lend to everyone, one hour at a time.

shot.visual_intent: A drawn table builds row by row: partition (mono) · max time · a bar whose length is the hours (8, 2, 2, 24, 24, 1); gpu-short's row gets a small ink 'prioritised' tag; sharing's row a kraft 'lent by PIs' tag. Act title top-left.

beats.narration_text: Which cards live in a partition? Ask sinfo for the G R E S column. On the gpu partition the answer is a mix: V100s in two flavours, T4s, A100s in two node sizes, and H200s, eight to a node. The number after the card is how many sit in each node.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Before you submit, it pays to know what's free. sinfo with the node list, the GRES and the GRES in use shows that per node. And to check one node, name it. One trap: a node in the MIXED state isn't telling you about its GPUs. MIXED describes its CPUs. Only the GRES-used column says whether a card is free.

beats.narration_text: There's also a GPU Monitor app on Open OnDemand. It colours every GPU node as idle, mixed or allocated, and lists how many GPU jobs are waiting in the queue by card type, so you can pick a card with a shorter line.

beats.narration_text: So what is a GPU? Start with a core: one unit that runs instructions on its own. A CPU has a few large, complex cores. A GPU has thousands of small, simple ones. For a problem you can split into thousands of identical little pieces, the GPU is the right tool.

beats.narration_text: Two pictures from the training. Delivering thousands of pizzas across a city: a few Ferraris, or thousands of bicycles? The bicycles. Or a room of professors at whiteboards against a stadium of students with calculators. The professors win at a hard proof. But to multiply a very large matrix, a multiply and an add for every cell, the stadium wins. Machine learning, scientific simulation, data analysis: those are stadium jobs.

beats.narration_text: Three ways to use them. Open OnDemand, a website where a GPU session is a form. An interactive session from the terminal with s run. And a batch job, a script you submit with s batch and walk away from.
beats.motion_claim: Three routes, each landing as one large library icon.

beats.narration_text: One setup for all three. Log in, go to your scratch directory, and clone the training repository. Everything the demos use is in there: a Python environment script, a tiny GPU check, and the example code.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: First way: the browser. On the Open OnDemand dashboard, open Standard Apps and pick VS Code Server.

beats.narration_text: When the session connects, open the cloned folder in VS Code, then a terminal from the View menu. Make the environment script executable, run it, and check that which python points into the new environment. Then the smallest possible test: the script prints the CUDA visible devices variable. Zero means the scheduler gave you a GPU.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Second way: a live session from the terminal. s run on the sharing partition with one GPU drops you onto a GPU node. Activate the same environment and run the fuller check, which asks PyTorch for the card.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Here's that check. It prints the PyTorch version, whether CUDA is available, the GPU's name, and then puts a tiny tensor on the card and prints where it lives. Open it in v i, add an NVIDIA S M I line, and run it again to see the card itself.

props.title: example1/gpu_test_torch.py
props.code:
import torch

print("Torch version:", torch.__version__)
print("CUDA available:", torch.cuda.is_available())
print("GPU name:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], device="cuda")
print("Tensor device:", x.device)
props.sparkLine: Four prints and one tensor on the card.

beats.motion_claim: The training's own code prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Third way: batch. The same work as a script with S BATCH lines: the gpu partition, one GPU, four CPUs, sixteen gigabytes, one hour, and log files. It activates the environment and runs the check. Submit it with s batch; it runs when a card is free, writes its output to the logs folder, and you read it later.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Is the card actually working? Put NVIDIA S M I in your script to print its state while the job runs. And after a job finishes, gpu-logs with the job ID gives a minute-by-minute record. This real one from the training: for five minutes nothing. Then memory climbs to twenty-three percent, then seventy-eight, with utilization still zero: the model is loading. Only at the end does utilization reach fifty-six percent. Most of this job's time, the GPU was waiting.

beats.narration_text: Two habits keep a GPU busy. First, batching. The naive version sends fifty thousand single rows to the card, one request at a time, and pays the overhead fifty thousand times.

props.title: example2/naive.py
props.code:
model = torch.nn.Linear(2048, 2048).to(device)
data_size = 50000

start = time.time()
# 50,000 separate requests to the GPU: lots of overhead
for _ in range(data_size):
    data = torch.randn(1, 2048).to(device)
    _ = model(data)

torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"Naive Time: {time.time() - start:.4f}s")

beats.motion_claim: The training's own code prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: The batched version sends all fifty thousand rows at once and runs the model once. Same arithmetic, far less overhead, and the card's thousands of cores all have work.

props.title: example2/optimized.py
props.code:
model = torch.nn.Linear(2048, 2048).to(device)
data_size = 50000

start = time.time()
# send all the data at once
data = torch.randn(data_size, 2048).to(device)
_ = model(data)

torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"Optimized Time: {time.time() - start:.4f}s")

beats.motion_claim: The training's own code prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Picture it. Fifty thousand tiny parcels through the door one at a time, the card idle between each. Or one crate, and every core busy at once.

beats.narration_text: Second, data loading. With zero workers the CPU prepares one batch at a time and the GPU waits for each. With workers, pinned memory and a non-blocking copy, the next batch is ready before the card finishes the current one. Batch your data. Give the loader workers. Keep the card working.

props.title: example2_cifar/loaders.py
props.code:
# naive: num_workers=0, the CPU loads one batch at a time
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=256, num_workers=0)
for images, labels in loader:
    images = images.to("cuda")          # GPU sits idle waiting

# optimized: workers in parallel, pinned memory, non-blocking copy
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=256, num_workers=2,
                    pin_memory=True)
for images, labels in loader:
    images = images.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)   # GPU stays busy

beats.motion_claim: The training's own code prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Four habits to leave with. Choose the right partition: gpu-short for a quick job, and s batch for anything long. Request only what you need, and check a finished job with seff to see how many CPUs it really used. Use the GPU-tuned libraries, CUDA and cuDNN, rather than plain code. And profile before you optimise. Stuck? Email r c help at northeastern dot e d u, or come to office hours.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Six GPU partitions; gpu-short schedules fast, and sharing is lent by PIs. sinfo with the G R E S column shows the cards, and the GRES-used column, not MIXED, says what's free. A GPU is thousands of simple cores: the stadium, not the professors. Three ways in: VS Code on Open OnDemand, s run with one GPU, or an s batch script. gpu-logs shows the card's memory and utilization minute by minute. And batch your data and give the DataLoader workers, so the card stays busy.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Here is a PyTorch loop I run on a GPU: [paste it]. First, tell me whether it processes samples one at a time or in batches, and rewrite it to batch if it doesn't. Second, write the DataLoader line with workers and pinned memory. Third, write me the Slurm srun command for a one-hour test on one GPU and the sbatch script for the real run. Then check two things yourself. Did it keep the arithmetic identical when it batched? And did it ask for only one GPU?
